claim: NIH 3T3 fibroblasts moved inside a fluorescently labelled cell derived matrix (CDM).
source: In our experiment, NIH 3T3 fibroblasts moved inside a fluorescently labelled cell derived matrix (CDM) (Figure 1a, left panels and Video 1), obtained using a protocol adapted from (Cukierman et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript directly states that NIH 3T3 fibroblasts moved inside a CDM, supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1a and Video 1.

claim: The CDM was obtained using a protocol adapted from Cukierman et al., 2001.
source: In our experiment, NIH 3T3 fibroblasts moved inside a fluorescently labelled cell derived matrix (CDM) (Figure 1a, left panels and Video 1), obtained using a protocol adapted from (Cukierman et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly cites Cukierman et al., 2001 as the source of the adapted protocol.

claim: A confluent monolayer of NIH3T3 cells expressing fluorescently labeled fibronectin was triggered to synthesize ECM proteins for 8 days.
source: Briefly, a confluent monolayer of NIH3T3 cells expressing fluorescently labeled fibronectin was triggered to synthesize ECM proteins for 8 days.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure used to generate the CDM.

claim: Cells were removed by lysis, generating a 3D protein meshwork.
source: Then, cells were removed by lysis, generating a 3D protein meshwork (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the lysis step and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1a showing the resulting meshwork.

claim: The resulting CDM had large pores inside, but it was covered by a dense crust.
source: The resulting CDM had large pores inside, but it was covered by a dense crust, as shown by electron microscopy (EM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the CDM structure as observed by electron microscopy.

claim: 3T3 fibroblasts seeded on top of the CDM passed through and spread within the matrix.
source: Despite this, 3T3 fibroblasts seeded on top of the CDM passed through and spread within the matrix, which was significantly thicker than cells themselves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: The manuscript describes cell behavior and references supporting figures.

claim: The CDM was significantly thicker than cells themselves.
source: Despite this, 3T3 fibroblasts seeded on top of the CDM passed through and spread within the matrix, which was significantly thicker than cells themselves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: The manuscript states this comparison and references supporting figures.

claim: Optical tweezer experiments showed no hysteresis in the displacement curves.
source: Optical tweezer experiments showed no hysteresis in the displacement curves, suggesting that the matrix behaved as an elastic material within the amplitudes and timescales explored (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and g), which is in agreement with previous reports (Petrie et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from optical tweezer experiments.

claim: The matrix behaved as an elastic material within the amplitudes and timescales explored.
source: Optical tweezer experiments showed no hysteresis in the displacement curves, suggesting that the matrix behaved as an elastic material within the amplitudes and timescales explored (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and g), which is in agreement with previous reports (Petrie et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript infers elastic behavior from the absence of hysteresis and cites supporting literature.

claim: The relationship between force and displacement was linear.
source: Moreover, the relationship between force and displacement was linear (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h) and we could determine the CDM's elastic modulus to be ≈50 Pa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h and i) and no modification of the meshwork was observed after 24 hr of cell migration inside (Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental measurements showing a linear relationship.

claim: The CDM's elastic modulus is approximately 50 Pa.
source: Moreover, the relationship between force and displacement was linear (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h) and we could determine the CDM's elastic modulus to be ≈50 Pa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h and i) and no modification of the meshwork was observed after 24 hr of cell migration inside (Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: The manuscript reports the measured elastic modulus value.

claim: No modification of the meshwork was observed after 24 hr of cell migration inside.
source: Moreover, the relationship between force and displacement was linear (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h) and we could determine the CDM's elastic modulus to be ≈50 Pa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h and i) and no modification of the meshwork was observed after 24 hr of cell migration inside (Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of the meshwork over time.

claim: These physiological 3D porous matrices were thick enough to host 3D cell migration.
source: Altogether, these physiological 3D porous matrices were thick enough to host 3D cell migration and were sufficiently soft and elastic to relate cell dynamics to matrix deformation.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the properties of the CDM based on the experimental characterization.

claim: The matrices were sufficiently soft and elastic to relate cell dynamics to matrix deformation.
source: Altogether, these physiological 3D porous matrices were thick enough to host 3D cell migration and were sufficiently soft and elastic to relate cell dynamics to matrix deformation.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the properties of the CDM based on the experimental characterization.

claim: Cells displayed an elongated morphology typical of fibroblasts in soft and elastic matrices.
source: Cells displayed an elongated morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), typical of fibroblasts in these soft and elastic matrices (Cukierman et al., 2001; Petrie et al., 2012; Caballero et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes observed cell morphology and cites supporting literature.

claim: Cells showed a cortical distribution of acto-myosin.
source: We observed (i) a cortical distribution of acto-myosin (Figure 1a), (ii) the presence of focal adhesions distributed all over the cell membrane and mediating its adhesion to the surrounding matrix (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 3), and (iii) the microtubule cytoskeleton expanding from the centrosome to the periphery of the cell (Figure 1d and Video 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from imaging experiments.

claim: Focal adhesions were distributed all over the cell membrane and mediated adhesion to the surrounding matrix.
source: We observed (i) a cortical distribution of acto-myosin (Figure 1a), (ii) the presence of focal adhesions distributed all over the cell membrane and mediating its adhesion to the surrounding matrix (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 3), and (iii) the microtubule cytoskeleton expanding from the centrosome to the periphery of the cell (Figure 1d and Video 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from imaging experiments.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton expanded from the centrosome to the periphery of the cell.
source: We observed (i) a cortical distribution of acto-myosin (Figure 1a), (ii) the presence of focal adhesions distributed all over the cell membrane and mediating its adhesion to the surrounding matrix (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 3), and (iii) the microtubule cytoskeleton expanding from the centrosome to the periphery of the cell (Figure 1d and Video 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from imaging experiments.

claim: The CDM was easily deformed by cells as they moved through.
source: Strikingly, the CDM was easily deformed by cells as they moved through (Figure 1a, right panels and Video 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of matrix deformation during cell migration.

claim: Matrix deformation was quantified via the Kanade-Lucas-Tomasi (KLT) tracker method.
source: This enabled us to quantify the associated matrix deformation (Delanoë-Ayari et al., 2008) via the Kanade-Lucas-Tomasi (KLT) tracker method (Lucas and Kanade, 1981; Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method used for quantification and cites the relevant literature.

claim: Deformations were present at the front and at the back of the nucleus of polarized cells, where phases with both contractile and extensile patterns were observed.
source: These deformations were present at the front and at the back of the nucleus of polarized cells, where phases with both contractile and extensile patterns were observed.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of deformation patterns in cells.

claim: Similar patterns were observed in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and rat embryo fibroblasts 52 (REF52) migrating in CDMs.
source: Similar patterns were also observed in other cell types migrating in CDMs. Both mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and rat embryo Fbroblasts 52 (REF52) exhibited phases of contraction and extension patterns at the front and the back of the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations in additional cell types.

claim: A transient densification of the myosin signal forming clusters of myosin was associated with the contraction observed in the matrix displacement.
source: We could observe a transient densification of the myosin signal forming clusters of myosin associated with the contraction observed in the matrix displacement (Figure 1c and Video 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlated observations of myosin clustering and matrix contraction.

claim: Enlargement of pores of the fibronectin meshwork suggested a local pulling force by the cells.
source: This force transmission between the cell and the CDM was also observed at the focal contact level: enlargement of pores of the fibronectin meshwork suggested a local pulling force by the cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript infers pulling forces from observed pore enlargement.

claim: Cells embedded in CDMs generate forces which translate into contractile and extensile deformations in the surrounding matrix.
source: Therefore, cells embedded in CDMs generate forces which translate into contractile and extensile deformations in the surrounding matrix.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the observations of force generation and matrix deformation.

claim: Some cells showed persistent motion while others moved back and forth along a constant central position.
source: During migration experiments, some cells showed persistent motion (Video 7) while others moved back and forth along a constant central position.
evidence: The manuscript describes two distinct types of cell behavior observed in experiments.

claim: Both migrating and non-migrating cells exhibited local zones of contraction-extension along time.
source: Interestingly, both migrating and non-migrating cells exhibited local zones of contraction-extension along time (Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations common to both cell types.

claim: Contraction-extension regions can be seen on both sides of the nucleus.
source: Such regions can be seen on both sides of the nucleus (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the spatial distribution of contraction-extension regions.

claim: For non-migrating cells, sequences of positive and negative divergence were observed on still regions at both sides of the nucleus.
source: For non-migrating cells, we could observe sequences of positive and negative divergence along time (alternating blue and yellow area) on still regions (black lines in Figure 2d) at both sides of the nucleus.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal pattern of divergence in non-migrating cells.

claim: These contraction-extension regions are equivalent to two force dipoles on either side of the nucleus.
source: Thus, we suggest that these contraction-extension regions are equivalent to two force dipoles on either side of the nucleus.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an interpretation of the observed contraction-extension patterns.

claim: The contraction-extension cycles were cyclic.
source: As it can be seen from the kymographs, these deformations were cyclic.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal nature of the deformations.

claim: Autocorrelation of the divergence profile for individual non-migrating cells resulted in periods of oscillation of approximately 6 min at the front and back of the cell.
source: Autocorrelation of the divergence profile for individual non-migrating cells (Figure 2f – representative example for one cell) resulted in periods of oscillation similar at the front and back of the cell (≈6 min) (Figure 2g) (see Materials and methods section for quantification of the oscillations).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of oscillation periods.

claim: For individual migrating cells, autocorrelation of divergence profiles gave oscillation periods of approximately 8 min, similar at the front and the back.
source: For individual migrating cells, autocorrelation of divergence profiles (Figure 2h – representative example for one cell) gave oscillation periods of ≈8 min, similar at the front and the back as well (Figure 2i).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of oscillation periods.

claim: These contraction relaxation cycles with periods of approximately 8 min and amplitudes of typically 2.5 µm are reminiscent of previous reports of cell autonomous contractile oscillations.
source: These contraction relaxation cycles with periods of ≈8 min and amplitudes of typically 2.5 µm are reminiscent of previous reports of cell autonomous contractile oscillations (Kruse and Riveline, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript compares the observed oscillations to previously reported phenomena.

claim: Periods of oscillations were comparable for motile and non-motile cells.
source: Periods of oscillations were comparable for motile and non-motile cells (Figure 2g and i).
evidence: The manuscript compares oscillation periods between cell types.

claim: The phases of contraction seemed to correlate with the formation of local myosin clusters.
source: The phases of contraction seemed to correlate with the formation of local myosin clusters as described above (Figure 1c), which is consistent with the observation of distinct myosin-driven contraction centers in the migration of neurons on 2D surfaces (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation between contraction and myosin clustering and cites supporting literature.

claim: Non-migrating cells systematically showed no phase shift between the two ends, with cross-correlation peaks localized at a time shift t=0.
source: While non-migrating cells systematically showed no phase shift between the two ends, with cross-correlation peaks localized at a time shift t=0, migrating cells showed cross-correlation peaks at non-zero time lags (Figure 2k), suggesting a phase shift between the front and back contraction-extension cycles (differences of phase shift in migrating and non-migrating cells were statistically significant with p=0.0246).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of cross-correlation showing no phase shift in non-migrating cells.

claim: Migrating cells showed cross-correlation peaks at non-zero time lags, suggesting a phase shift between the front and back contraction-extension cycles.
source: While non-migrating cells systematically showed no phase shift between the two ends, with cross-correlation peaks localized at a time shift t=0, migrating cells showed cross-correlation peaks at non-zero time lags (Figure 2k), suggesting a phase shift between the front and back contraction-extension cycles (differences of phase shift in migrating and non-migrating cells were statistically significant with p=0.0246).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of cross-correlation showing phase shift in migrating cells.

claim: Differences of phase shift in migrating and non-migrating cells were statistically significant with p=0.0246.
source: While non-migrating cells systematically showed no phase shift between the two ends, with cross-correlation peaks localized at a time shift t=0, migrating cells showed cross-correlation peaks at non-zero time lags (Figure 2k), suggesting a phase shift between the front and back contraction-extension cycles (differences of phase shift in migrating and non-migrating cells were statistically significant with p=0.0246).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of the phase shift differences.

claim: A system undergoing directed motion must exhibit time reversal asymmetry.
source: A system undergoing directed motion must exhibit time reversal asymmetry. In our case, this asymmetry manifests itself through a time lag between the contraction-extension cycles of the two force dipoles.
evidence: The manuscript states a physical principle and applies it to the observed system.

claim: The time reversal asymmetry manifests itself through a time lag between the contraction-extension cycles of the two force dipoles.
source: A system undergoing directed motion must exhibit time reversal asymmetry. In our case, this asymmetry manifests itself through a time lag between the contraction-extension cycles of the two force dipoles.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the observed time lag as a manifestation of time reversal asymmetry.

claim: The characterization of the mechanical properties of the CDM showed that it locally behaves as a linear elastic material with a well-defined elastic modulus.
source: Indeed, our characterization of the mechanical properties of the CDM showed that it locally behaves as a linear elastic material with a well-defined elastic modulus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f-j).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the mechanical characterization results.

claim: This supports the approximation of a linear relationship between the moments of the force distribution and the moments of the resulting matrix displacement distribution.
source: This supports the approximation of a linear relationship between the moments of the force distribution and the moments of the resulting matrix displacement distribution.
evidence: The manuscript infers a linear relationship based on the elastic properties of the CDM.

claim: The main dipole axis was aligned with the direction of motion within experimental noise.
source: The main dipole axis was aligned with the direction of motion – within experimental noise (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for a quantification) – as was reported for 2D motion (Tanimoto and Sano, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript reports the alignment of the main dipole axis with the direction of motion and cites supporting literature.

claim: The level of traction exerted by the cell on the matrix observed for non-migrating cells is comparable in magnitude to those of migrating cells.
source: The level of traction exerted by the cell on the matrix observed for non-migrating cells is comparable in magnitude to those of migrating cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b, differences between migrating and non-migrating cells are not statistically significant with p=0.2766).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparison of traction forces.

claim: The absence of migration is not due to the lack of traction forces.
source: This shows that the absence of migration is not due to the lack of traction forces (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript infers that lack of migration is not due to lack of traction based on the comparable traction forces.

claim: Trajectories showed a cycle enclosing a finite area for migrating cells, but a negligible area for non-migrating cells.
source: We indeed observe that trajectories showed a cycle enclosing a finite area for migrating cells, but a negligible area for non-migrating cells (Figure 3d and e, and more examples in Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of trajectories in the dipole-quadrupole phase space.

claim: A cell that underwent motion and then stopped showed cycles that switched from a finite area while the cell was moving to a vanishing area when the cell stopped.
source: Strikingly, we observed that the cycles switched from a finite area while the cell was moving to a vanishing area when the cell stopped (Figure 3h).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of a cell transitioning between migrating and non-migrating states.

claim: The finite area is a direct illustration of the fact that the phase shift between the contraction-extension cycles at the two ends of migrating cells also manifests itself in the pattern of matrix displacement.
source: The finite area is a direct illustration of the fact that the phase shift between the contraction-extension cycles at the two ends of migrating cells observed in Figure 2 also manifests itself in the pattern of matrix displacement.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the finite area as a manifestation of the phase shift.

claim: This is a clear signature of time reversal symmetry breaking.
source: This is a clear signature of time reversal symmetry breaking.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the finite area as evidence of time reversal symmetry breaking.

claim: Both absolute areas and normalized areas were substantially larger for migrating cells than for non-migrating cells.
source: Both absolute areas (in µm5/min2) and normalized areas (in percent of the area of the rectangle fitting the trajectory) were substantially larger for migrating cells than for non-migrating cells (differences were statistically significant with p=0.0177 and p=0.0431, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparison of cycle areas with statistical significance.

claim: The relevant difference between the two behaviors is the existence of a phase shift rather than a difference in the level of traction forces.
source: This supports our claim that the relevant difference between the two behaviors is the existence of a phase shift rather than a difference in the level of traction forces.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the results to support the importance of phase shift over traction force magnitude.

claim: Upon addition of nocodazole, cell migration stopped.
source: Upon addition of the drug, cell migration stopped (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of nocodazole treatment on cell migration.

claim: Some nocodazole-treated cells underwent a forward backward movement in the matrix.
source: Some cells then underwent a forward backward movement in the matrix (Video 9), which hinted at an oscillation driven by local force dipoles.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of cell behavior after nocodazole treatment.

claim: Nucleus-free cells (cytoplasts) underwent a forward backward movement in the CDM.
source: We observed a similar behavior in nucleus-free cells, generated when protrusions rupture from the cell. The resulting cytoplast underwent a forward backward movement in the CDM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c, Video 10).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of cytoplast behavior.

claim: Cytoplasts switched polarization over time, with a frequency of one direction reversal every approximately 36 min.
source: They switched polarization over time, with a frequency of one direction reversal every ≈36 min.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of cytoplast polarization switching.

claim: Nocodazole-treated cells showed a typical period of approximately 11 min.
source: Although the nocodazole-treated cells did not maintain a fixed cell polarization either, we extracted matrix displacement which showed a typical period as for non-treated cells of ≈11 min (Figure 2g).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of oscillation periods in nocodazole-treated cells.

claim: Oscillations at different cell ends were in phase in nocodazole-treated cells and cells did not show directed motion.
source: However, oscillations at different cell ends were in phase and cells did not show directed motion.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of oscillation phase and cell motion in nocodazole-treated cells.

claim: The coupling between oscillators needed to promote directed motion could involve microtubules.
source: This suggests that the coupling between oscillators needed to promote directed motion could involve microtubules.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a hypothesis based on the nocodazole treatment results.

claim: The microtubular network spans the entirety of the cell body and is a natural candidate to transfer information between the two ends of the cell.
source: Indeed, the microtubular network spans the entirety of the cell body (Figure 1d and Video 4), and is thus a natural candidate to transfer information between the two ends of the cell.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a role for microtubules based on their spatial distribution.

claim: The microtubular network regulates the polarity axis of migrating cells.
source: This suggestion is consistent with the notion that the microtubular network regulates the polarity axis of migrating cells (Etienne-Manneville, 2004; Kaverina and Straube, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature supporting the role of microtubules in cell polarity.

claim: The net velocity of both swimmers and crawlers decreases if the period of oscillation increases for oscillations of constant amplitude.
source: For oscillations of constant amplitude, the net velocity of both swimmers and crawlers decreases if the period of oscillation increases.
evidence: The manuscript states a prediction from the theoretical models.

claim: The instantaneous velocity oscillates around the average values given by Equations 1 and 2, with a time dependence that reflects the dynamics of the underlying force dipoles.
source: For such self-propelled objects, the instantaneous velocity oscillates around the average values given by Equations 1 and 2, with a time dependence that reflects the dynamics of the underlying force dipoles.
evidence: The manuscript states a prediction from the theoretical models.

claim: Experimental observations report strong oscillations of the instantaneous cell velocity.
source: Experimental observations indeed report strong oscillations of the instantaneous cell velocity (Figure 4c).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observations of velocity oscillations.

claim: For WT cells, velocity and period showed a clear anticorrelation.
source: To test how the period of oscillation of migrating cells influenced their velocity, we took advantage of the inherent variability of cells and plotted the velocity vs. period for WT cells and observed a clear anticorrelation (Figure 4d).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of the relationship between velocity and period.

claim: This is consistent with locomotion being driven by controlling cell deformation instead of cell traction forces.
source: Although the large cellular noise prevented us from quantitatively comparing the scaling relations given by Equations 1 and 2, this is consistent with locomotion being driven by controlling cell deformation instead of cell traction forces.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the anticorrelation as supporting a specific mechanism of locomotion.

claim: Similar conclusions have been reached in the different context of adherent epithelial cells.
source: Similar conclusions have been reached in the different context of adherent epithelial cells (Saez et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature reporting similar findings in a different cell type.

claim: All pharmacological treatments altered cell migration.
source: As expected, all pharmacological treatments altered cell migration.
evidence: The manuscript reports the general effect of drug treatments on cell migration.

claim: Latrunculin A and nocodazole stalled migration completely.
source: Latrunculin A (Video 12) and nocodazole (Video 9) stalled migration completely.
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific effects of these drugs on cell migration.

claim: Speed oscillations were observed for cells treated with Y-27632, ML-7, C8-BPA, and CK666.
source: Among the others, we observed speed oscillations for cells treated with Y-27632, ML-7, C8-BPA, and CK666.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of oscillations in drug-treated cells.

claim: Those treatments reduced persistent cell speed.
source: Those treatments reduced persistent cell speed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i) and increased the period of speed oscillations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1j), showing that we could indeed alter cell migration behavior.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative effects of drug treatments on cell speed.

claim: Those treatments increased the period of speed oscillations.
source: Those treatments reduced persistent cell speed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i) and increased the period of speed oscillations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1j), showing that we could indeed alter cell migration behavior.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative effects of drug treatments on oscillation period.

claim: An inverse correlation between period and velocity is evident at the population level, both for WT cells and when those are aggregated to pharmacologically treated cells.
source: Therefore, an inverse correlation between period and velocity is evident at the population level, both for WT cells and when those are aggregated to pharmacologically treated cells.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the overall relationship between period and velocity across conditions.

claim: The temporal coupling between spatially distributed force dipoles along the cell promotes cell motion.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the temporal coupling between spatially distributed force dipoles along the cell promotes cell motion.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism based on the experimental results.

claim: Localized laser ablation within the cortex of a cell triggered the relaxation of the cell and the surrounding matrix.
source: We observed that localized laser ablation within the cortex of a cell (Figure 5a and b before ablation) triggered the relaxation of the cell and the surrounding matrix, as marked by the displacement of the matrix away from the cut region (Figure 5b ablation).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from laser ablation experiments.

claim: This process was then followed by a contraction of the cell along with the surrounding matrix.
source: This process was then followed by a contraction of the cell along with the surrounding matrix (Figure 5b after ablation).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from laser ablation experiments.

claim: Laser ablation led to the transient recruitment of actin and myosin.
source: Remarkably, laser ablation led to the transient recruitment of actin and myosin (Figure 5c bottom left and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), which co-localized with cell contraction (Figure 5c bottom right and Video 13).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of protein recruitment following laser ablation.

claim: For a polarized cell the laser-induced contraction triggered the translocation of the cell.
source: For a polarized cell the laser-induced contraction triggered the translocation of the cell (Figure 5b), whereas for a cell with no clear polarization and multiple attachment points no cell body translocation was observed (Figure 5c).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of cell translocation following laser ablation in polarized cells.

claim: For a cell with no clear polarization and multiple attachment points no cell body translocation was observed.
source: For a polarized cell the laser-induced contraction triggered the translocation of the cell (Figure 5b), whereas for a cell with no clear polarization and multiple attachment points no cell body translocation was observed (Figure 5c).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of lack of translocation in non-polarized cells following laser ablation.

claim: By laser ablation we could induce matrix pinching that could lead to a cell translocation given certain cell morphology.
source: Therefore, by laser ablation we could induce matrix pinching that could lead to a cell translocation given certain cell morphology.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the results of laser ablation experiments.

claim: Repeatedly locally imposing cellular force dipoles by triggering local contractions alternatively at the front and the back of a polarized cell triggered reiterated translocation and led to a net movement of the cell.
source: So, we then used this method to repeatedly locally impose cellular force dipoles, by triggering local contractions alternatively at the front and the back of a polarized cell (see schematics in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b). We imposed correlated contractions by selecting a constant time interval between consecutive laser ablations: this triggered reiterated translocation and led to a net movement of the cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and Video 14).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from repeated laser ablation experiments.

claim: This externally induced cell displacement was achieved when laser ablation of equal power was applied sequentially at the front and the back of the nucleus, both with about 6 and 10 min intervals between cuts.
source: This externally induced cell displacement was achieved when laser ablation of equal power was applied sequentially at the front and the back of the nucleus, both with about 6 and 10 min intervals between cuts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the conditions under which externally induced displacement was achieved.

claim: When sequential ablation was applied repeatedly only at one side of a polarized cell (front), net displacement was either absent or smaller than when alternating front and back.
source: In contrast, when this sequential ablation was applied repeatedly only at one side of a polarized cell (front), net displacement was either absent or smaller than when alternating front and back, both with about 5 and 10 min intervals between cuts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The manuscript reports control experiments showing the importance of alternating ablation sites.

claim: Externally induced force dipoles are sufficient to promote directed cell motion.
source: This shows that externally induced force dipoles are sufficient to promote directed cell motion and illustrates that by alternating induced force dipoles at front and back of the nucleus leads to net cell motion.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the laser ablation results as demonstrating sufficiency of force dipoles for directed motion.

claim: By alternating induced force dipoles at front and back of the nucleus leads to net cell motion.
source: This shows that externally induced force dipoles are sufficient to promote directed cell motion and illustrates that by alternating induced force dipoles at front and back of the nucleus leads to net cell motion.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the laser ablation results as demonstrating the importance of alternating dipoles.

claim: This supports the principle of a phase shift between local dipoles as a trigger for cell motility.
source: Altogether, this supports the principle of a phase shift between local dipoles as a trigger for cell motility.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the laser ablation results as supporting the phase shift mechanism.

claim: Acto-myosin complexes are likely to be the functional elements that control the dynamics of the individual contractile units.
source: Acto-myosin complexes are likely to be the functional elements that control the dynamics of the individual contractile units.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a role for acto-myosin complexes based on the observations.

claim: The cycles of protrusion/retraction at both ends of the cell likely involves transient retrograde actin flow whose periodic nature could be linked to a stick-slip phenomenon.
source: The cycles of protrusion/retraction at both ends of the cell likely involves transient retrograde actin flow whose periodic nature could be linked to a stick-slip phenomenon (Sens, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism for the observed cycles and cites supporting literature.

claim: The absence of a coherent actin flow at the scale of the entire cell and the existence of multiple competing protrusions considerably slows down cell motion.
source: Therefore, although the local actin dynamics within protrusions could be comparable to that fast moving cells in 2D or under confinement (Barnhart et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2015), the absence of a coherent actin flow at the scale of the entire cell and the existence of multiple competing protrusions considerably slows down cell motion.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an explanation for slow cell motion and cites supporting literature.

claim: For cells moving in 3D CDMs, the lack of time reversal symmetry required for cell motion is associated with a time shift between the oscillating dynamics of the two cell ends.
source: Our results show that for cells moving in 3D CDMs, the lack of time reversal symmetry required for cell motion is associated with a time shift between the oscillating dynamics of the two cell ends.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The dynamics of individual dipoles appear similar in migrating and non-migrating cells.
source: Remarkably, the dynamics of individual dipoles appear similar in migrating and non-migrating cells, suggesting that the same force generation machinery is equally active in both types of cells, and that it is the synchronization between individual units that makes movement possible.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the observations to suggest similar force generation machinery in both cell types.

claim: The same force generation machinery is equally active in both types of cells.
source: Remarkably, the dynamics of individual dipoles appear similar in migrating and non-migrating cells, suggesting that the same force generation machinery is equally active in both types of cells, and that it is the synchronization between individual units that makes movement possible.
evidence: The manuscript infers equal activity of force generation machinery from similar dipole dynamics.

claim: It is the synchronization between individual units that makes movement possible.
source: Remarkably, the dynamics of individual dipoles appear similar in migrating and non-migrating cells, suggesting that the same force generation machinery is equally active in both types of cells, and that it is the synchronization between individual units that makes movement possible.
evidence: The manuscript proposes that synchronization is the key factor enabling movement.

claim: Altering the dynamics of individual units can affect motion, in particular, faster oscillations can lead to faster motion.
source: Altering the dynamics of individual units can affect motion, in particular, faster oscillations can lead to faster motion, but the coordination between units is key in enabling cell translocation.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the relationship between oscillation dynamics and motion.

claim: The coordination between units is key in enabling cell translocation.
source: Altering the dynamics of individual units can affect motion, in particular, faster oscillations can lead to faster motion, but the coordination between units is key in enabling cell translocation.
